question: For a simple undirected graph with N vertices given by its adjacency matrix A: (1) what does the entry (A^k)_{ij} represent, (2) how can one determine from A whether the graph is connected, and (3) what is the definition of a path between vertices n_i and n_j?

claims.text: Textbook Lemma 1.2.1 is proved by induction on the length k of the walk. If a vertex repeats (u_i = u_j, i < j), the walk u_0, ..., u_i, u_{j+1}, ..., u_k is shorter than k, so the induction hypothesis gives a simple (u, v)-path from it. So the textbook's proof gives a path no longer than the walk.

claims.text: Lemma L1: if there is a (u, v)-walk of length k in a simple graph, with u and v equal or different, then there is a (u, v)-path (distinct vertices) of length at most k whose vertices and edges all belong to the walk. Proof by strong induction on k: if a vertex repeats, u_i = u_j with i < j, cut out the steps between and get a walk of length i + (k - j) < k with the same ends.

support.quote: Ենթադրենք, որ G գրաֆում u-ն և v-ն իրարից տարբեր երկու գագաթներ են։ Այդ դեպքում ցանկացած (u, v)-շրջանցումից կարելի է առանձնացնել պարզ (u, v)-ճանապարհ։

claims.text: Proposition P1: in a simple graph, a walk whose vertices are pairwise distinct has pairwise distinct edges, so every path is a trail. Proof: for steps a < b the vertex u_b is an end of the b-th edge but, being later in the list than u_{a-1} and u_a, it is not an end of the a-th edge.

claims.text: Proposition P2: for vertices u, v, the length of a shortest (u, v)-walk, of a shortest (u, v)-trail and of a shortest (u, v)-path are equal, and all are infinite together. So the textbook's distance d(u, v) (Definition 1.2.16, stated with the textbook's 'path', English trail) is the same whether read with trails or with paths, and equals the length of a shortest walk.

claims.text: The textbook does not state whether a walk of length 0 is allowed. This module reads it as allowed, because the textbook's own property d(u, u) = 0 needs a (u, u)-path of length 0, and Grinberg's Example 2.9.2 has a length-0 path. It does not count a length-0 closed trail as a cycle (the textbook's simple cycle C_n has n >= 3 and says nothing on k = 0).
